title: Ancient South Arabia
subtitle: 1,200–300 BC · Sabaʾ, Maʿīn, Qatabān and the Rise of the Incense Kingdoms

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The first states in the Arabian Peninsula — Sabaʾ's federator-priests and kings, and the rival caravan kingdoms of Maʿīn, Qatabān, Ḥaḍramawt and the doomed Awsān

entries.label: The mukarribs and the federation of Sabaʾ
entries.hint: Sabaʾ's early rulers held the title mukarrib — 'federator' — and bound a loose confederation of highland and desert-edge tribes together through the collective cult of the god Almaqah and periodic rituals of inclusion. It is the first organised state on the Arabian Peninsula.
entries.note: the Sabaean royal inscriptions of Sirwah and Marib; Christian Robin, 'Sabaʾ et ses rois', and Norbert Nebes on the mukarrib institution.

entries.label: Yathaʿʾamar Watar and the Assyrian synchronism
entries.loc: Marib · recorded in Sargon II's annals, Khorsabad
entries.hint: In 715 BC the annals of Sargon II of Assyria record tribute from 'Itʾamra the Sabaean' — almost certainly the mukarrib Yathaʿʾamar Watar. It is the earliest firmly datable event in South Arabian history and the peg on which the whole 'long chronology' hangs.
entries.note: the Khorsabad Annals of Sargon II; the identification is standard since Glaser — see Kitchen, 'Documentation for Ancient Arabia' (1994–2000).

entries.label: Karibʾil Watar, the conqueror
entries.hint: Karibʾil Watar bin Dhamarʿali left a long war-record inscription at Sirwah listing campaigns that destroyed Nashshan and Awsān, subdued the Jawf and pushed Sabaean power from Najran to the sea. A 'Karibʾilu king of Saba' also sent gifts to Sennacherib, fixing his date.
entries.note: RES 3945, the res gestae of Karibʾil Watar; Sennacherib's account of Arabian gifts. Nebes, 'Der Tatenbericht des Karibʾil Watar' (2016).

entries.label: From mukarrib to malik — the kings of Sabaʾ
entries.hint: By the 6th century BC Sabaean rulers had dropped the sacral title mukarrib for the plain 'malik', king of Sabaʾ — a shift from priest-federator to territorial monarch, ruling from Marib over an oasis kingdom rather than a ritual confederation.
entries.note: the later Sabaean royal titulary; Robin, 'Sabaʾ et ses rois', in Robin and Vogt (eds), 'Yémen: au pays de la reine de Saba' (1997).

entries.label: Awsān, the southern power broken by Sabaʾ
entries.hint: Awsān, in Wadi Markha, was briefly a leading power of the deep south, its kings later remembered with a semi-divine cult. Karibʾil Watar of Sabaʾ destroyed its capital around 680 BC; its distinctive royal statues were dug from the ruins two and a half millennia later.
entries.note: RES 3945 (the Sabaean account of Awsān's destruction); the Awsanite royal statues, now in Aden and European collections; Antonini and Agostini on Awsān.

entries.group: Maʿīn and the Jawf City-States (c.700–300 BC)
entries.label: The kingdom of Maʿīn at Qarnaw
entries.hint: Maʿīn was a kingdom built on commerce, not conquest: from Qarnaw and the walled town of Yathill (Baraqish) its merchant houses ran the incense road north, planting colonies as far as Dedan and Egypt. Its kings appear alongside a powerful council of merchants.
entries.note: the Minaean royal and commercial inscriptions; Alessandra Avanzini, 'Corpus of South Arabian Inscriptions I–III: Qatabanic, Marginal Qatabanic, Awsanite' and the Minaean corpus; Robin on Maʿīn.

entries.group: Maʿīn and the Jawf City-States (c.700–300 BC)
entries.label: The Jawf city-states — Nashshan, Kaminahu, Haram
entries.hint: Between Maʿīn and Marib the Wadi al-Jawf held a cluster of small walled caravan cities — Nashshan, Kaminahu, Haram, Nashqum — each with its own kings, temples and script variant, alternately independent and subject to Sabaʾ or Maʿīn.
entries.note: the Jawf city inscriptions; the French–Yemeni excavations at as-Sawda (Nashshan) and Kaminahu; Robin and Bron, 'Inventaire des inscriptions sudarabiques'.

entries.label: Qatabān and the kings at Timnaʿ
entries.hint: Qatabān, ruled from Timnaʿ in Wadi Bayhan, controlled a central stretch of the incense road and the approaches to the Bab al-Mandab. Its kings issued coinage and the earliest surviving market law in Arabia.
entries.note: the Qatabanic royal inscriptions; the American Foundation for the Study of Man excavations at Timnaʿ (Wendell Phillips, 1950–51); Avanzini, 'Corpus of South Arabian Inscriptions' (Qatabanic).

entries.label: Ḥaḍramawt and the gatekeepers of Shabwa
entries.hint: The kingdom of Ḥaḍramawt, ruled from Shabwa on the edge of the sands, held the frankincense-bearing valleys of the far south-east. Every caravan of incense had to pass through Shabwa and pay its tithe before heading north.
entries.note: the Ḥaḍramite royal inscriptions; the French archaeological mission at Shabwa (Jean-François Breton, Rémy Audouin); Pliny, Natural History XII, on the Shabwa tithe.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The war-record inscriptions of Sabaʾ, the erasure of Awsān, and a long three-cornered contest between Sabaʾ, Maʿīn and Qatabān for the caravan road

entries.label: Karibʾil Watar's campaigns of conquest
entries.loc: the Jawf, Wadi Markha and Najran
entries.hint: The Sirwah war-record claims campaign after campaign under Karibʾil Watar — Nashshan burned, its walls thrown down, tens of thousands killed or enslaved, Awsān annihilated, the Jawf cities made tributary. It is the founding text of Sabaean imperial memory.
entries.note: RES 3945; Nebes (2016). The casualty figures are the inscription's own claims and are not independently checkable.

entries.label: The destruction of Awsān
entries.hint: Sabaʾ razed the Awsanite capital and broke the kingdom so thoroughly that it vanished from history for four centuries. The surviving Awsanite royal statues, stiff and frontal, are almost all that is left of a power that had rivalled Sabaʾ itself.
entries.note: RES 3945; the Awsanite statuary in the National Museum, Aden, and the Musée du Louvre.

entries.label: The three-cornered contest for the road
entries.hint: After Sabaean hegemony faded, Sabaʾ, Maʿīn and Qatabān spent two centuries fighting over control of the caravan corridor and its toll revenue, with the Jawf cities and Ḥaḍramawt shifting allegiance between them. No one power could hold the whole route.
entries.note: reconstructed from the royal inscriptions of all three kingdoms; Robin, 'Sabaʾ et ses rois'; Avanzini on the Qatabanic–Sabaean frontier.

entries.label: The walled caravan towns
entries.hint: Every caravan city was a fortress: Baraqish's oval wall with its fifty-odd towers still stands nearly complete, and Marib, Timnaʿ and the Jawf towns were all ringed in ashlar masonry. Endemic raiding and inter-kingdom war made the wall the normal condition of urban life.
entries.note: the standing wall of Baraqish (Yathill); Breton, 'Les fortifications d'Arabie méridionale du 7e au 1er siècle avant notre ère' (1994).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Sacral kingship, oasis water law, the market regulation of Timnaʿ and the frankincense tithe of Shabwa — government in the caravan kingdoms was mostly the government of trade and water

entries.label: The Almaqah cult as the constitution of Sabaʾ
entries.hint: The mukarrib governed by ritual: leading the pilgrimage to Almaqah's temple, staging the ceremonies that periodically re-admitted tribes to the federation, and performing the sacred hunt. Political membership of Sabaʾ was defined by participation in the cult.
entries.note: Nebes on the mukarrib institution; Robin, 'Le calendrier sabéen' and 'Sabaʾ et ses rois'.

entries.label: The Marib oasis water regime
entries.hint: The dam's floodwater was divided between a northern and a southern oasis through a system of canals, distributors and sluice gates, administered by named officials and recorded in inscriptions. Water rights, not land, were the fundamental property of the Sabaean economy.
entries.note: the Marib irrigation inscriptions; the German Archaeological Institute's Marib oasis surveys (Brunner, Gerlach).

entries.label: The market law of Timnaʿ
entries.hint: A long Qatabanic royal inscription set up at the Timnaʿ market regulates it in detail: who may trade, the king's dues on sales, the treatment of foreign merchants, penalties for fraud. It is the earliest commercial statute known from Arabia.
entries.note: RES 3878, 'the market law of Timnaʿ'; translations in Beeston, 'The Qatabanic Market Law', and Avanzini's Qatabanic corpus.

entries.label: The frankincense tithe at Shabwa
entries.hint: Frankincense harvested in Ḥaḍramawt had to be brought to Shabwa, where the priests of the god Sayin took a tenth off the top before the caravans were allowed to proceed. It was a state tax collected as religion, funding both temple and crown.
entries.note: Pliny the Elder, Natural History XII.63–65, on the Shabwa tithe; the French mission's work on Shabwa's warehouses.

entries.label: Maʿīn's law over its merchants abroad
entries.hint: Maʿīn maintained legal authority over its citizens far from home — regulating the marriages, property and obligations of Minaean traders resident at Dedan, in Egypt and around the Mediterranean, and recording their affairs on inscriptions back in the Jawf.
entries.note: the Minaean commercial and 'hierodule' inscriptions; K. A. Kitchen and Avanzini on the Minaean diaspora texts.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: A shared pantheon headed by ʿAthtar, a national god for each kingdom, pilgrimage to the great oval temples, the sacred hunt, and the public confession of ritual faults

entries.label: ʿAthtar and the national gods
entries.hint: Every South Arabian kingdom shared the astral god ʿAthtar at the head of its pantheon, then set its own national deity below him: Almaqah for Sabaʾ, Wadd for Maʿīn, ʿAmm and Anbay for Qatabān, Sayin for Ḥaḍramawt. Religion and political identity were the same thing.
entries.note: Jacques Ryckmans and Christian Robin on the South Arabian pantheon; the standard synthesis in 'Yémen: au pays de la reine de Saba' (1997).

entries.label: The temple of Almaqah at Awwam
entries.hint: The oval precinct of Awwam, its great curtain wall enclosing a pillared hall, was the federal sanctuary of Sabaʾ and the goal of its annual pilgrimage. Thousands of dedicatory inscriptions from the temple are a primary archive of Sabaean society.
entries.note: the American Foundation for the Study of Man excavations at the Maḥram Bilqīs (1951–52, resumed 1998); Glanzman and the AFSM reports.

entries.label: Pilgrimage and the sacred hunt
entries.loc: Marib and the highland game reserves
entries.hint: The Sabaean year turned on a pilgrimage to Almaqah and on a ritual hunt of ibex and gazelle, performed by the ruler to secure rain and the land's fertility. The hunt appears again and again in the inscriptions and on the temple reliefs.
entries.note: Robin, 'Le calendrier sabéen'; Serjeant, 'South Arabian Hunt' (1976), on the ritual hunt and its survival into recent times.

entries.label: The confession inscriptions
entries.loc: the temples of Marib and the Jawf
entries.hint: Worshippers who had broken a ritual rule — entering the sanctuary in a state of impurity, breaking a sexual taboo — publicly confessed the offence on an inscribed bronze or stone plaque and paid a fine to the god. Many of the confessants are women.
entries.note: the South Arabian 'expiation' or 'confession' texts; Sima, 'Die sabäischen Bußinschriften'; Robin on the genre.

entries.label: The votive economy of the temples
entries.hint: Vows fulfilled with bronze statuettes, alabaster plaques, incense altars and slaves poured into the great temples, which became the largest landowners and creditors in their kingdoms. The temple was a bank, an archive and a court as much as a place of sacrifice.
entries.note: the dedicatory inscription corpora of Awwam and the Minaean temples; Maraqten on temple administration in ancient Yemen.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Monumental ashlar architecture, the geometric Musnad script, stylised alabaster faces, near-life-size bronzes and a repeating grammar of ibex friezes and false windows

entries.label: The great temples of Marib and the Jawf
entries.loc: Awwam and Bar'an, near Marib, Yemen
entries.hint: South Arabian builders worked in finely dressed ashlar, without mortar, raising peristyle halls on tall monolithic pillars — the Bar'an temple's five standing pillars are the emblem of ancient Yemen. The style spread unchanged from Marib to the Jawf and across the sea to Yeha.
entries.note: the DAI excavations at Bar'an (al-Masajid) and Awwam; Schmidt, 'Der Tempel des Waddum dhu-Masmaʿim'.

entries.label: The Musnad script as a visual system
entries.hint: The monumental South Arabian script — tall, strictly geometric letters of even weight, first written boustrophedon then left-to-right — was designed for the chisel. Its regularity makes South Arabian inscriptions instantly recognisable and, unusually, closely datable by letter form.
entries.note: Jacques Ryckmans, 'L'ordre alphabétique sud-sémitique'; Peter Stein on South Arabian palaeography.

entries.label: Alabaster funerary heads and stelae
entries.loc: Timnaʿ, Marib and the Jawf, Yemen
entries.hint: South Arabian tombs were marked with alabaster faces — broad, flat, geometric, the eyes once inlaid with shell and lapis or paste — and with name-stelae in Musnad. Mass-produced yet individually named, they are the region's most recognisable art.
entries.note: the alabaster stelae in the museums of Aden, Sanaa, the Louvre and the British Museum; Antonini, 'Scul­ture sudarabiche'.

entries.label: The bronze statuary of Awwam
entries.hint: Sabaean bronzeworkers cast near-life-size human figures for the temple, including the famous pair dedicated by a man named Maʿadkarib. The scale and the confident modelling put South Arabian bronze casting on a level with the contemporary Mediterranean.
entries.note: the Maʿadkarib bronzes and related figures from the Maḥram Bilqīs; AFSM excavation records; Simpson (ed.), 'Queen of Sheba' (2002).

entries.label: The ibex frieze and the false-window motif
entries.hint: A standard decorative grammar runs through South Arabian building and furniture: rows of ibex horns, dentil courses, and the recessed 'false window' panel. It is consistent enough to trace the culture's reach and to date buildings by their ornament.
entries.note: Antonini and Avanzini on South Arabian architectural decoration; the ibex-frieze fragments in the Sanaa and Aden museums.

entries.label: Lyres, pipes and the temple banquet
entries.hint: Carved stelae and bronze plaques show seated figures playing lyres and double pipes at banquets, and bronze cymbals and rattles turn up in temple deposits. Music accompanied both the ritual feast and the funerary cult.
entries.note: banqueting stelae from Timnaʿ (AFSM excavations); instrument depictions catalogued in Simpson (ed.), 'Queen of Sheba' (2002).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: An internal record in stone and palm-wood, and the beginnings of an outside geography of 'Arabia Felix' by the Greeks

entries.label: The long-and-short chronology problem
entries.hint: Dating the Sabaean mukarribs has divided scholarship for a century: a 'long chronology' anchored on the Assyrian synchronisms of 715 and 685 BC, against a 'short chronology' that once brought Karibʾil Watar down to the 5th century. Palaeography and radiocarbon now favour the long version.
entries.note: the history of the debate from Glaser and Rhodokanakis to Pirenne's 'Paléographie des inscriptions sud-arabes' (1956); recent resolution in Kitchen (1994–2000) and Nebes (2016).

entries.label: The zabur wooden documents
entries.loc: the Wadi al-Jawf and Nashshan, Yemen
entries.hint: Alongside the monumental script, South Arabians wrote an everyday minuscule cursive on palm-leaf stalks and wooden sticks: letters, loans, contracts, and children's writing exercises. Their decipherment revealed a broadly literate society, not just a monument-carving elite.
entries.note: Peter Stein, 'Die altsüdarabischen Minuskelinschriften auf Holzstäbchen' (2010); Yūsuf Muḥammad ʿAbd Allāh and the Sanaa collection.

entries.label: The Greeks discover Arabia Felix
entries.loc: Athens and Alexandria · reporting on South Arabia
entries.hint: Theophrastus described the frankincense and myrrh trees around 300 BC from traders' reports; Eratosthenes and then Agatharchides mapped the incense kingdoms and their wealth. 'Arabia Felix' — fortunate, or simply southern — enters Mediterranean geography.
entries.note: Theophrastus, Enquiry into Plants IX; Agatharchides of Cnidus, On the Erythraean Sea (preserved in Photius and Diodorus).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Oasis irrigation feeding the capitals, the frankincense groves of the south-east, and the caravan road that carried their produce two thousand kilometres to the Mediterranean

entries.label: The Marib oasis
entries.hint: The floodwater of the Great Dam irrigated some ninety square kilometres of the Marib oasis in two great fields, the largest area of artificial cultivation anywhere in ancient Arabia. It fed the Sabaean capital and made the whole caravan-kingdom model possible.
entries.note: the DAI Marib oasis project (Brunner, Gerlach); Charloux and Schiettecatte on South Arabian oasis agriculture.

entries.label: The Jawf and Wadi Bayhan irrigation
entries.loc: Wadi al-Jawf and Wadi Bayhan, Yemen
entries.hint: Maʿīn and Qatabān built their own runoff-irrigation systems in the Jawf and Wadi Bayhan — smaller than Marib's but on the same principle, spreading silt-laden flash floods across bunded fields to grow the grain that fed the caravan towns.
entries.note: Avanzini and the Italian mission's surveys of the Wadi Bayhan; the French mission in the Jawf.

entries.label: Frankincense and myrrh
entries.hint: The Boswellia trees of Ḥaḍramawt and Dhofar and the Commiphora of the south yielded the ancient world's supply of frankincense and myrrh — burned in every temple from Babylon to Rome. South Arabia's monopoly on the source is the foundation of its wealth.
entries.note: Groom, 'Frankincense and Myrrh' (1981); Pliny, Natural History XII, on the harvest and the routes.

entries.label: The incense road toll economy
entries.loc: the caravan road, Shabwa to Najran
entries.hint: Every kingdom the caravans crossed levied dues, water charges and protection payments; Pliny reckoned the cost of moving frankincense to the Mediterranean at nearly its own weight in silver. The temples and city walls of ancient Yemen were built on that toll.
entries.note: Pliny, Natural History XII.63–65; Nigel Groom's route reconstruction; Schiettecatte, 'D'Aden à Zafar'.

entries.label: The Minaean merchant houses
entries.loc: from Qarnaw to Dedan, Egypt and the Aegean
entries.hint: Maʿīn ran the northern end of the trade as a commercial network: Minaean merchant families resident at Dedan, in the Egyptian Fayyum, at Gaza, and a Minaean altar dedicated on Delos. It is the earliest documented long-distance trading diaspora from Arabia.
entries.note: the Minaean inscriptions of Dedan (al-ʿUlā); the Delos altar (Minaean dedication to Wadd); Minaean names in Egyptian sources — Kitchen (2000).

entries.label: Camels, gold and stones for the northern courts
entries.loc: South Arabia · reaching Nineveh and Babylon
entries.hint: Assyrian and Babylonian records list camels, gold, precious and semi-precious stones, and aromatics coming from 'the Sabaeans'. South Arabia was plugged into the Near Eastern luxury market from the 8th century BC, a full participant rather than a curiosity.
entries.note: the Assyrian royal annals (Tiglath-Pileser III, Sargon II, Sennacherib); Ephʿal, 'The Ancient Arabs' (1982).

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The Great Dam of Marib, the alphabet in two registers, and the pack-camel logistics that made a desert trade route pay

entries.label: The Great Dam of Marib
entries.date: c.1700–700 BC (monumental phase from c.700 BC)
entries.hint: An earthen barrier some 720 metres long threw Wadi Dhana's floods sideways into two masonry sluice complexes, the North and South Sluices, which fed the oasis canals. Rebuilt again and again against silt and flood, it stood for well over a thousand years.
entries.note: the DAI Marib Dam studies (Brunner, 'Die Erforschung der antiken Oase von Marib'); the standing North and South Sluice structures.

entries.label: The South Arabian alphabet, monumental and minuscule
entries.hint: The 29-consonant Musnad abjad — a South Semitic branch of the alphabet — came in two registers: the geometric monumental script for stone and bronze, and a flowing minuscule for palm-wood. The same society read and wrote in both.
entries.note: Ryckmans on the South Semitic alphabetic order; Stein (2010) on the minuscule; the abecedaries from Raybun and elsewhere.

entries.label: Pack camels and caravan logistics
entries.hint: The domesticated dromedary and a shoulder-borne pack saddle turned the waterless interior into a highway: caravans of hundreds of camels, moving between fixed wells and walled way-stations, could carry incense from Shabwa to Gaza in about seventy days.
entries.note: Bulliet, 'The Camel and the Wheel' (1975); Groom (1981) on caravan stages and timings.

entries.label: Silt management and the rising oasis
entries.loc: the Marib and Bayhan oases, Yemen
entries.hint: South Arabian irrigators deliberately let each flood drop its silt on the fields, raising the cultivated surface by metres over the centuries and forcing constant heightening of the canals and sluice gates. The oasis was an engineered landform, not just watered ground.
entries.note: Gerlach and Brunner on the Marib oasis stratigraphy; the metres-deep anthropogenic silt of the Marib fields.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: A 2,000-kilometre caravan road to the Mediterranean, a merchant colony at Dedan, a daughter-civilisation across the Red Sea in Ethiopia, and a Hebrew memory of the Queen of the South

entries.label: The Incense Road as a system
entries.loc: Shabwa – Timnaʿ – Marib – Najran – Dedan – Gaza
entries.hint: The overland route ran from the Ḥaḍramawt groves through each kingdom's capital in turn, up the western edge of Arabia to Dedan and Yathrib, and on to Gaza and the sea — with an eastern branch to Gerrha on the Gulf. It is the deep ancestor of the classical caravan geography.
entries.note: Groom, 'Frankincense and Myrrh' (1981); Pliny, Natural History XII; the way-station archaeology along the Wadi al-Jawf–Najran corridor.

entries.label: Dʿmt — South Arabia across the Red Sea
entries.hint: South Arabian colonists and influence created the Ethio-Sabaean kingdom of Dʿmt in the northern Ethiopian highlands. The temple of Yeha, raised around 700 BC in pure South Arabian ashlar and inscribed in Sabaic, still stands twelve metres high.
entries.note: the German–Ethiopian excavations at Yeha (DAI, Wolbert Smidt, Iris Gerlach); Nebes, 'Die Inschriften aus dem Almaqah-Tempel in Meqaber Gaʿewa'.

entries.label: The Minaean quarter at Dedan
entries.hint: At Dedan, the northern hinge of the incense road, Minaean merchants formed a resident community with their own inscriptions and cult, living alongside the Dadanite and then Lihyanite kingdom that hosted them. The road created diaspora settlements at both ends.
entries.note: the Minaean inscriptions of al-ʿUlā; Farès-Drappeau, 'Dédan et Liḥyān' (2005); the Saudi–European surveys of the al-ʿUlā oasis.

entries.label: Assyria, Babylon and Persia
entries.loc: South Arabia · and the Mesopotamian courts
entries.hint: South Arabian rulers sent tribute and gifts to Sargon II and Sennacherib, traded into Nebuchadnezzar's Babylon, and fell within the notional reach of the Achaemenid road system. The caravan kingdoms managed relations with every great power to their north.
entries.note: the Assyrian annals; Ephʿal, 'The Ancient Arabs' (1982); Herodotus III.107–113 on Arabian incense and the Persian tribute.

entries.label: The Queen of Sheba tradition
entries.hint: The account of the queen of Sabaʾ visiting Solomon with camels bearing spices, gold and gems, and Sheba recurring in the prophets as a byword for caravan wealth, is a Hebrew memory of contact with the incense trade — later elaborated across three religions.
entries.note: 1 Kings 10:1–13 and 2 Chronicles 9; Ezekiel 27:22–23, Isaiah 60:6, Psalm 72:10, 15; Job 6:19. Simpson (ed.), 'Queen of Sheba' (2002), on the tradition's growth.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The Arabian Peninsula's first states appear in the south, built on an engineered oasis in a drying land — and by the end of the folio the trade that made them is starting to move to the sea

entries.label: The rise of the caravan kingdoms
entries.loc: the southern highlands and desert edge, Yemen
entries.hint: Between about 1000 and 700 BC a cluster of literate, temple-centred, irrigation-based states — Sabaʾ, Maʿīn, Qatabān, Ḥaḍramawt, Awsān — takes shape in the south. They are the first states anywhere on the Arabian Peninsula, and they run on trade.
entries.note: Robin, 'Sabaʾ et ses rois'; Schiettecatte, 'Les villes de l'Arabie du Sud aux époques préislamiques'.

entries.label: An irrigation civilisation in a drying land
entries.loc: Marib and the Ramlat as-Sabatayn margins, Yemen
entries.hint: South Arabian civilisation was a standing fight against the environment: the monsoon that fed the dam was weakening, the wadis ran only in flash floods, and the oasis silted up as fast as it was watered. Prosperity depended on unbroken collective maintenance.
entries.note: Lézine on the Holocene monsoon decline; Brunner on the dam's maintenance cycles.

entries.label: From Sabaean hegemony to a balance of powers
entries.hint: Karibʾil Watar's 7th-century Sabaʾ briefly dominated the whole south; by the 5th century that had settled into a stable multipolar system of four kingdoms sharing the road, a balance that lasted until Himyar upset it three centuries later.
entries.note: Robin, 'Sabaʾ et ses rois'; Avanzini, 'By land and by sea: a history of South Arabia before Islam' (2016).

entries.label: The thread continues — the sea route and the rise of Himyar
entries.loc: the Red Sea and the southern highlands
entries.hint: From the 3rd century BC, Ptolemaic and then Roman shipping began working the Red Sea directly, slowly undercutting the overland toll economy. Around 110 BC a new power, Himyar, rose in the southern highlands — the subject of the next folio.
entries.note: a forward reference: south-arabia-300bc-628 (Sabaean–Himyarite wars to the eve of Islam) is planned but not yet built. On the sea shift, Sidebotham, 'Berenike and the Ancient Maritime Spice Route' (2011).

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Women named and propertied in the inscriptions, foreign brides in the Minaean diaspora, the anxieties recorded on the confession plaques, and the dependent labour under the oasis

entries.label: Women in the South Arabian inscriptions
entries.loc: Marib, Qarnaw and the Jawf, Yemen
entries.hint: South Arabian women dedicate statues in their own names, hold and transfer property, and appear as legal persons in the texts — within a patrilineal society, but with a visibility rare in the ancient Near East. Some Minaean inscriptions are commissioned by women alone.
entries.note: Maraqten, 'Women's inscriptions from ancient South Arabia'; Robin on the legal status of South Arabian women.

entries.label: The Minaean 'hierodule' lists
entries.hint: A set of Minaean inscriptions lists women — many named as being from Gaza, Egypt, Dedan, Ammon and Moab — brought into Minaean households or temple service. Whether marriage records, manumissions or dedications, they document cross-cultural unions along the trade road.
entries.note: the Minaean 'Hierodulenlisten' (M 392 and related); the interpretation is debated — Rhodokanakis, Beeston, and more recently Multhoff and Stein.

entries.label: Ordinary belief on the confession plaques
entries.loc: the temples of Marib and the Jawf, Yemen
entries.hint: The expiation inscriptions are one of the few ancient sources that record the religious anxieties of non-elite people — mostly about sexual and menstrual purity, mostly women — in their own words, prompted by illness or misfortune read as divine punishment.
entries.note: Sima, 'Die sabäischen Bußinschriften'; see the Belief entry on the genre.

entries.label: Dependent labour under the oasis
entries.loc: the Marib and Bayhan oases, Yemen
entries.hint: The canals, sluices and fields were built and maintained by corvée and by dependent and enslaved labour attached to the crown and the temples. Slaves are among the objects dedicated to the gods in the votive inscriptions.
entries.note: the dedicatory inscriptions listing dedicated slaves; Maraqten on labour and temple estates in ancient Yemen.
